title: UI students build technology for global neutrino experiment
excerpt: Work underway inside the University of Iowa Spaceflight Laboratory will eventually become part of one of the world’s largest particle physics experiments.Studen
content:
IOWA CITY, Iowa — Work underway inside the University of Iowa Spaceflight Laboratory will eventually become part of one of the world’s largest particle physics experiments.

Students are assembling electronics for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, or DUNE, an international project studying neutrinos and what the particles could reveal about the universe.

“We're building components for the DUNE Neutrino experiment. DUNE is a worldwide collaboration of about 1500 physicists,” University of Iowa physics professor Jane Nachtman said.

The University of Iowa team is producing 700 electrical shielding boxes and 350 electronic circuit boards for the experiment’s light detection system. Researchers at the university have spent about a decade developing and prototyping components for DUNE before moving into the current production phase.

The work gives students experience assembling equipment that must meet specific requirements before it leaves Iowa. Nachtman said students are learning about engineering, quality control, electronics and debugging throughout the process.

“This is a really once in a lifetime opportunity to be part of the construction of this detector,” Nachtman said.

Sophomore Hassler Ramirez is one of the students working on the shielding boxes. He described a multistep process that includes installing pieces, tightening components to specific measurements and preparing the boxes to eventually connect to the detector.

Ramirez said the scale and expected lifespan of the project make the experience stand out.

“I think that it's crazy that we're building a detector that lasts for such a long time, and it's going to discover so many different types of sciences and help us understand the universe and how it works,” Ramirez said.

At the center of DUNE’s research are neutrinos, particles that constantly pass through matter but rarely interact with it.

“Neutrinos are very mysterious particles. They're all around us. They're going through all the time, trillions every second, but they so rarely interact that you will never know,” Nachtman said.

Scientists know neutrinos can change between three different types, known as “flavors.” Studying those changes allows researchers to measure properties of the particles and look for clues about how the universe is structured.

The University of Iowa team is about a quarter of the way through its work on the electrical shielding boxes. Nachtman said the team expects to finish those around Thanksgiving, with the circuit boards following a similar timeline.

After leaving Iowa, the components will go through additional stages of assembly before becoming part of the detector at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota.

The detector will be assembled roughly a mile underground in a former gold mine, where researchers will study particles that rarely interact with other matter.

Once production in Iowa is complete, the components built by students in Iowa City will become part of a much larger detector assembled with contributions from scientists and institutions around the world.
